title: Fill Enclosed Pockets
statement:
A board is a grid of "#" (solid) and "." (open) cells. Open cells that share a side (up, down, left or right) form one pocket. A pocket is enclosed if none of its cells lies on the outer edge of the board.

Change the board in place: fill every enclosed pocket, turning all its cells into "#". Pockets that reach the edge stay as they are. Return nothing.

Corner contact does not connect cells, so a pocket that touches an edge cell only diagonally is still enclosed.

examples.why: The three-cell pocket in the middle touches no edge, so it is filled. The cell (2, 4) is on the right edge and (3, 1) is on the bottom edge, so both stay open.
The pocket looks closed in, but its cell (3, 2) is on the bottom edge. One edge cell keeps the whole pocket open, so nothing changes.
The pocket (1, 1)–(1, 2) touches the open corner cell only diagonally, which does not connect, so it is filled.

hints: Deciding for each pocket whether it is enclosed is awkward. Which pockets are easy to recognise for certain?
Every pocket that survives contains at least one open cell on the edge. Start from those edge cells.
Flood from every open edge cell and mark what you reach as safe. Then sweep the board: open cells that were not marked are enclosed and get filled; marked cells go back to open.

explain.intuition:
The rule is about whole pockets, but you do not need to examine each pocket. Flip the question: instead of "which pockets are enclosed?", ask "which open cells can reach the edge?". Those are exactly the cells connected to some open cell on the edge. A flood fill seeded with every open edge cell finds them all in one pass.

Everything open that the flood did not reach is enclosed, so it gets filled. Marking with a temporary value such as "S" (safe) keeps it in place: no extra visited grid is needed, and a final sweep turns "." into "#" and "S" back into ".". It is the same as a paint bucket that fills from the outside in, then inverts.
steps: Push every open cell on the top and bottom rows and the left and right columns into a queue, marking each "S".
BFS: pop a cell and mark each open neighbour "S" and push it.
Sweep the whole board: "." becomes "#" (enclosed), "S" becomes "." (safe).
Return nothing; the board was changed in place.
pitfalls: Filling cells while you are still deciding. If you check one cell at a time and fill it, later cells of the same pocket lose their path to the edge. Decide first, then fill in a separate sweep.
Treating a pocket as safe because it touches an edge cell diagonally. Example 3 is filled even though it sits next to an open corner.
Recursive flood fill from the edges. A snake-shaped pocket on a 200 × 200 board can be 20 000 cells deep, which is past Python's recursion limit. Use a queue or a stack.

solutions.title: Check each open cell on its own
solutions.idea: For every open cell, run a search over open cells to see whether it reaches the edge. Record the answer, then fill afterwards. Correct, but the same pocket is searched once per cell.

solutions.title: Flood from the edges, then sweep
solutions.idea: Mark every open cell reachable from an open edge cell as safe with one BFS. Then fill whatever is still open and restore the safe cells.

followups: Instead of filling, return the number of enclosed pockets and the size of each.
The board is a torus: the left edge wraps to the right and the top to the bottom. What does "enclosed" mean now, and how does the search change?
